claim: What existed passes and what did not exist arises; grief cannot change this, so grieving serves nothing.

heals.why: Grief is shown to have no power over what has already changed, which frees the energy it was holding
Loss of position is placed inside the ordinary coming and going of things

cultivates.why: Seeing that things arise and pass is the view the sage wants the prince to stand on

needs: That the loss is final and cannot be argued back

commentary.reading: The sage tells a prince who has lost his kingdom that possession is by nature unstable, so sorrow over it has no purchase. It is counsel on lost wealth and position, not on a death.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Desire only what can be had, enjoy what is present, and do not grieve over what has not come.

heals.why: Turns attention from what has not arrived to what is actually here
Limits wanting to what is reachable

cultivates.why: Enjoying what is present is named as the practice

commentary.reading: Kalakavrikshiya's practical counsel to the deposed prince: stop longing for the unattainable, use what is at hand.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: As a churned lake clears by itself, a person of formed understanding regains clarity from within.

heals.why: The churning is pictured as temporary and self-settling
Agitation is shown as a disturbed surface, not the nature of the water

cultivates.why: Clarity returns from within when understanding has matured

commentary.reading: The clearing is said of the kritaprajna, one whose understanding is formed; it is wisdom that settles the mind, not the mere passing of time.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

line_issue: Line says 'a mind, given time'; the verse says a person of formed wisdom clears by himself. Corrected: 'A churned-up lake clears by itself. So does a person whose understanding has ripened.'

claim: The cane bends before the flood and stands again when it passes; yielding in time preserves you.

heals.why: Shows a way through overwhelming force that does not require breaking

cultivates.why: Resilience is pictured as bending and returning to one's place
Reading the time and the strength of what is coming

needs: That the force faced is truly stronger and temporary

commentary.reading: Bhishma's answer on how a weak king survives a stronger enemy: bow at the right time, recover when the force has passed. Statecraft counsel, not a rule to submit to mistreatment.
commentary.source: Bhishma's sarit-sagara-samvada, Shanti Parva Rajadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Where the beloved is, even the foot of a tree is home; without her a palace is a wilderness.

depicts.why: Spoken by the pigeon waiting through a storm for a mate who has not come home

cultivates.why: Names what a partner's presence is actually worth

commentary.reading: The pigeon's lament for his missing wife; the passage praises the wife as the true home of a householder.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Hospitality is owed even to an enemy who arrives at your home, as a tree shades its cutter.

cultivates.why: Care for one who arrives in need, whoever he is
The tree image holds back retaliation

needs: The story: a guest in need has come to one's door

commentary.reading: This is atithi-dharma: the duty to a guest who has come seeking shelter, upheld by the pigeon even toward the fowler who caged his mate. It is not a general rule to be kind to whoever harms you.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

line_issue: Line generalises guest-duty into 'be kind even to one who wronged you'. Corrected: 'Welcome even an enemy who comes to your door. A tree does not pull back its shade from the one who comes to cut it.'

claim: Even the sole ruler of the whole earth has only one stomach, so more possession adds little.

heals.why: Shows the hard limit on what any amount of having can be used for
The one who has everything still eats one meal

cultivates.why: Enough is measured by need, not by reach

commentary.reading: Yudhishthira, sick of the war's cost, argues against Bhima's praise of kingship. The whole arc matters: his brothers, Draupadi and Vyasa answer him and he does take up the rule.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Keep a grateful mind and a friendly spirit, for everything comes through a friend.

heals.why: Points a lonely reader back to the worth of the friends they have

cultivates.why: Gratitude is named as the disposition to hold
Friendship is called the source of every good

commentary.reading: Bhishma's moral to the story of Gautama, who killed the crane that had fed and enriched him: ingratitude to a friend has no expiation, so be kritajna.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: You have fallen from happiness into sorrow and will reach happiness again; neither lasts forever.

depicts.why: Addresses a father directly as one who has fallen from happiness into sorrow

heals.why: Sorrow is placed in a turning cycle, with return promised
Denies that the present state is permanent

cultivates.why: Footing to wait out the turn

commentary.reading: The brahmin to King Senajit, grieving his son: sukha and duhkha turn like a wheel and no one holds either always.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Idleness is pleasant and ends in sorrow; capable effort is hard and brings happiness and prosperity.

heals.why: Names the trade: ease now, sorrow later

cultivates.why: Fortune is said to live with the capable

commentary.reading: Daksha, the capable and diligent person, is the home of Shri; the idle are not.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Whether what comes is pleasant or painful, receive it with a heart that is not defeated.

heals.why: Offers the stance of the undefeated heart in place of collapse
Whatever arrives can be met

cultivates.why: Aparajita hridaya, the undefeated heart, is the quality named
Pleasant and unpleasant are received alike

commentary.reading: Counsel to the grieving king: attend to each thing as it arrives, inwardly unconquered.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Countless occasions for grief and fear enter the unwise every day, but not the wise.

heals.why: Locates the flood of worry in how the mind receives events
Fear's occasions are many, their entry is not inevitable

cultivates.why: Discernment is what keeps the occasions from entering

commentary.reading: The verse calls the one overwhelmed a mudha, a person without discernment; it recurs across the epic as a stock consolation.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

line_issue: Line drops that the verse contrasts the unwise with the wise, and reads as gentler than the text. Corrected: 'Every day a thousand reasons for grief and a hundred for fear arrive. They overrun the unthinking mind, not the wise one.'

claim: Neither worldly pleasure nor heavenly joy equals a sixteenth of the happiness of craving ended.

heals.why: Sets the end of wanting above every object of wanting
Pleasure is ranked far below freedom from the pull

cultivates.why: Happiness is relocated from getting to no longer needing
Makes letting go the larger gain

needs: Some taste of the tiredness of wanting

commentary.reading: A much-quoted verse: trishna-kshaya-sukha outweighs kama-sukha and divya-sukha.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: One who has dropped expectation sleeps in peace; Pingala found that freedom from expectation is the highest ease.

heals.why: The waiting itself is shown as the pain, and its end as rest
Sleep returns when the outcome is no longer gripped

cultivates.why: Letting the expected thing go
Ease is pictured as a night of sleep

needs: Asha here is clinging to one awaited person or outcome, not hope in life

commentary.reading: Pingala waited all night for a lover who did not come, saw the misery of hanging on another, and let go. Nairashya is freedom from craving expectation.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Do today what is due tomorrow, because death does not wait for your work to be finished.

heals.why: Removes the assumption that there will be time later
Calls drift what it is

cultivates.why: Begin the thing now

commentary.reading: Medhavin means the work of one's highest good, shreyas and dharma, which his father keeps postponing behind worldly stages. The text says death, not time.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

line_issue: Line replaces death with 'time'. If the mortality gate allows, use: 'Do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's in the morning. Death does not wait to see if it is done.'

claim: While a person stays absorbed in the done and the undone, death takes hold of him.

depicts.why: The inner list of done, pending and half done is voiced from inside
A mind that never leaves its tasks

heals.why: Shows busyness as a form of sleep

commentary.reading: Medhavin to his father: the man attached to the pleasure of striving is seized by Kritanta, death, mid-task.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

line_issue: Line softens death to 'life slips by'. Acceptable as a gated variant; faithful version: 'This is done, this is next, this is half done. While we are busy like this, death arrives.'

claim: Knowledge is the best eye, truth the best austerity, attachment the worst sorrow, letting go the best happiness.

heals.why: Clinging is named the greatest sorrow

cultivates.why: Tyaga is named the greatest happiness
Knowledge is called the eye

commentary.reading: A summary maxim of the Mokshadharma; raga is attachment and tyaga its giving up.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Desire is born of one's own imagining, and ends at the root when the imagining stops.

heals.why: Traces desire to its root in dwelling on the object
Shows wanting is fed, not fated

cultivates.why: Seeing the mechanism is itself the release
Refusing to feed the thought

commentary.reading: Manki addresses Kama directly after losing his last bullocks: desire arises from sankalpa, the mind's projecting and dwelling. Sankalpa here is not 'resolve'.
commentary.source: Manki Gita, Shanti Parva Mokshadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: I will forgive those who abuse me, not injure those who injure me, and answer hatred with kind words.

heals.why: A spoken vow not to return injury
Refuses to carry the other's hatred forward

cultivates.why: Forgiveness taken as a personal vow
Kind speech toward the hostile

needs: A reader who is choosing non-retaliation freely, not one being pressed to accept mistreatment

commentary.reading: Manki has renounced all striving and speaks as one leaving the world; this is a renunciate's vow, not a householder's rule for dealing with injustice.
commentary.source: Manki Gita, Shanti Parva Mokshadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Having hands is the greatest gain; a creature without them longs for hands as you long for wealth.

heals.why: Shows the humiliated man what he still holds
Answers a wish to give up with the worth of a human body
Turns the eye from the rich man to his own capacity

cultivates.why: Hands, and what they can do, as the first wealth
Capacity to act is the gain

commentary.reading: Kashyapa, struck down by a rich man's chariot, resolves to die; Indra as a jackal shows him the worth of human birth. The story carries a self-harm theme.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Royal fortune stays with no one; it sat with thousands before and has only moved to you.

heals.why: Success is shown as a visitor, not a possession
The fallen speaker keeps his dignity by seeing fortune's nature

cultivates.why: Rise and fall both belong to fortune's movement
Bali answers mockery without bitterness or grovelling

commentary.reading: Bali, fallen and mocked by Indra, replies calmly that Shri is fickle and Kala brings each his turn. The dignity of the reply is the teaching.
commentary.source: Bali-Vasava-samvada, Shanti Parva Mokshadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Joy and sorrow, gain and loss, life and death reach everyone in turn, so be neither bewildered nor elated.

heals.why: Loss is one turn of a wheel everyone rides
The same wheel forbids getting carried away

cultivates.why: Neither crushed nor carried away is the instruction

commentary.reading: Vyasa cites Senajit to Yudhishthira: all receive these opposites paryayatah, by turns.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Days, months and years do not return, and beings once parted do not meet again.

heals.why: Makes the unrepeatable nature of time vivid

cultivates.why: Seeing that time moves one way
Meetings are understood as temporary by nature

commentary.reading: Ashma teaches Janaka that Kala carries all beings; union is like travellers meeting on a road. It is a teaching on bearing loss through seeing impermanence.
commentary.source: Ashma Gita, Shanti Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

line_issue: 'Be here for the ones in front of you' is not in the verse. Corrected: 'Days do not come back, nor months, nor years. Those who part do not meet again as they were.'

claim: A person becomes old, sorrowful and alone in an empty world when parted from his mother.

depicts.why: Says exactly what losing a mother does: one is suddenly old and the world is empty
The emptiness of the world without her

commentary.reading: Chirakari, ordered by his father to kill his mother, reflects at length on what a mother is; his slowness saves her and his father blesses it.
commentary.source: Chirakari upakhyana, Shanti Parva Mokshadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: There is no shade, refuge, protection or loved one equal to a mother.

depicts.why: For one who has lost her, it names the size of the loss

cultivates.why: Names what a mother has been: shade, refuge, protection

commentary.reading: Part of Chirakari's praise of the mother while he deliberates.
commentary.source: Chirakari upakhyana, Shanti Parva Mokshadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Form a friendship slowly and end one slowly, because a slowly made friendship endures.

cultivates.why: Take time before binding or breaking a bond
Slow friendship is the lasting kind

commentary.reading: Gautama's praise of deliberateness after his son's slowness prevented a killing ordered in anger.
commentary.source: Chirakari upakhyana, Shanti Parva Mokshadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: In passion, pride, hostility and when a close one's fault is unclear, the one who acts slowly is praised.

heals.why: Delay is given as the specific answer to anger's first order
Permits not deciding until the facts are clear

cultivates.why: Slowness is praised exactly where judgement is most clouded

commentary.reading: Gautama had ordered his wife killed on a suspicion; his son's delay let the truth surface. The verse lists kin, friends, servants and women as those whose unproven faults deserve slow judgement.
commentary.source: Chirakari upakhyana, Shanti Parva Mokshadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

line_issue: Sanskrit lists 'women' beside servants; the line's neutral 'a loved one' is right and should be kept. No rewrite needed.

claim: The one without anger is superior to the angry, the forbearing to the unforbearing, the knowing to the ignorant.

heals.why: Ranks restraint above the flare of anger

cultivates.why: Titiksha is named the higher quality

commentary.reading: The Hamsa ranks qualities for the Sadhyas; a generic ranking maxim.
commentary.source: Hamsa Gita (Sadhya-Hamsa samvada), Shanti Parva Mokshadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: A person becomes like those he keeps company with and like what he wishes to be, as cloth takes its dye.

heals.why: Makes visible a slow influence one usually does not notice

cultivates.why: Company is shown as the dye; choosing it is choosing oneself
What one wishes to become is counted among the shaping forces

commentary.reading: Satsanga teaching: character follows association and aspiration.
commentary.source: Hamsa Gita (Sadhya-Hamsa samvada), Shanti Parva Mokshadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

line_issue: Line omits 'what one wishes to become'. For aspiration plans: 'You become like the people you keep company with, and like what you wish to be, the way cloth takes the colour of its dye.'

claim: Silence is better than idle speech; if one speaks, let it be true, then righteous, then also kind.

heals.why: Gives a checklist to run before speaking in heat

cultivates.why: Four filters for speech
Kindness is the finishing quality of true speech

commentary.reading: Gita Press reads these as successive excellences of speech: not speaking, then truthful, then dharmic, then pleasing. The order of the last two differs between recensions.
commentary.source: Hamsa Gita (Sadhya-Hamsa samvada), Shanti Parva Mokshadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: Do not strike at another's tender spots or speak cruelly; never say the scorching word that makes someone recoil.

heals.why: Names the exact act to hold back: the word that wounds

cultivates.why: Asks one to feel the other's flinch before speaking

commentary.reading: Arun-tuda is one who pierces the marma, the vital spot. The same verse is in Vidura Niti. 'Na hinatah param abhyadadita' is usually read as not overcoming another by base means.
commentary.source: Hamsa Gita (Sadhya-Hamsa samvada), Shanti Parva Mokshadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: Word-arrows strike another's vital spots and leave him grieving day and night, so the wise never loose them.

depicts.why: The one hit by words is pictured grieving night and day

heals.why: Shows the lasting cost of the angry sentence

cultivates.why: Sees speech from the receiver's side

commentary.reading: The Hamsa's warning on harsh speech; also in Vidura Niti. For a person wounded by words the first half validates the wound.
commentary.source: Hamsa Gita (Sadhya-Hamsa samvada), Shanti Parva Mokshadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: Truthful speech is good, but speech that serves the lasting good of beings is higher and is the real truth.

heals.why: Resolves the bind between honesty and kindness by ranking the good of the other first

cultivates.why: Tests words by whether they help
Truth is measured by the welfare of beings

commentary.reading: Sanatkumara's definition as passed by Narada: satya is what is finally for the good of beings. Not a licence for convenient untruth.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Sorrow that cannot be remedied is best treated by not dwelling on it, since brooding makes it grow.

heals.why: Rumination is named as what feeds the pain
Gives permission to stop replaying what cannot be changed

cultivates.why: Withholding attention from the loop is the practice

needs: That nothing more can be done about the cause

commentary.reading: Narada to Shuka: bhaishajyam etad duhkhasya, this is sorrow's medicine. The next verses limit it to what effort cannot change.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Mental pain should be destroyed by wisdom and bodily pain by medicine; one should not behave like the childish.

heals.why: Assigns the mind's pain its own proper remedy
Says understanding can treat what medicine cannot

cultivates.why: Knowing which remedy fits which pain

commentary.reading: Prajna for manasa duhkha, aushadha for sharira duhkha; the closing words tell the hearer not to be like the unthinking.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

line_issue: 'Both deserve care' is added and the mild rebuke is dropped. Corrected: 'Meet the mind's pain with understanding and the body's pain with medicine. That is what knowledge is for.'

claim: Grieving over what is dead or lost adds a second sorrow to the first.

heals.why: Separates the loss from the added pain of replaying it
Shows the loop as a second misfortune one can decline

commentary.reading: Narada to Shuka: one who mourns the past gains sorrow through sorrow and meets two evils.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: When an undertaking fails, do not torment yourself; apply yourself again, which is the highest policy.

heals.why: Forbids self-torment over a failed attempt
Failure is treated as a moment in the work, not its end

cultivates.why: Renewed exertion is called the supreme rule
Keep applying yourself

commentary.reading: Bhishma opens Rajadharma with utthana, exertion: a king must not burn over a failed enterprise but strive again.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: A wrong once done is destroyed by good action, by confession, remorse, giving and austerity.

heals.why: Says a wrong is not final and names the ways it is worked off

cultivates.why: Turns remorse into specific acts

commentary.reading: Yudhishthira cites the doctrine of prayashchitta while arguing that he should renounce; the second half is bracketed in the edition as a variant. His family answers that his duty is to rule, and he does.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: The best friend is one not pained by your rise and more saddened than you at your decline.

heals.why: Holds up the friend who is glad at another's rise

cultivates.why: A clear test for who is truly on your side
Describes the friend one can try to be

commentary.reading: Bhishma's marks of the uttama mitra, given so a king may know whom to trust.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Like the mother of two rival gamblers, I cannot wish victory for one or defeat for the other.

depicts.why: Krishna himself voices being torn between two sides of his own family
He speaks as one worn down by kinsmen's quarrels

commentary.reading: Krishna confides in Narada about the feud between the Vrishni factions; even he feels the bind. Narada then gives the 'weapon not made of iron'.
commentary.source: Vasudeva-Narada samvada, Shanti Parva Rajadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

line_issue: Line drops Krishna's own image. Better: 'I am like a mother whose two sons are gambling against each other. I cannot wish one to win, because the other must lose.'

claim: Feeding others as one can, forbearance, straightness, gentleness and due honour are the weapon not made of iron.

heals.why: Replaces the urge to fight kin with five concrete habits
Gives the one in the middle something to do

cultivates.why: Titiksha toward one's own people
Honouring each as is due
Feeding and giving within one's means

commentary.reading: Narada to Krishna as head of a quarrelling clan: win kinsmen with the soft weapon. Counsel to the one who holds responsibility for the family, not to one being abused in it.
commentary.source: Vasudeva-Narada samvada, Shanti Parva Rajadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: One who never speaks and always frowns is disliked; one who greets first with a smile wins goodwill.

heals.why: Gives a lonely person a first move: speak first, smile first

cultivates.why: Warm speech as a daily practice

commentary.reading: Brihaspati to Indra: santva, conciliatory speech, is the one quality that makes a person loved by all.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: A gift given without kind words does not please, like food without seasoning.

cultivates.why: Kind words are what make giving land

commentary.reading: Brihaspati on santva: speech completes generosity.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: As a person ages, hair, teeth, eyes and ears wear out, but craving alone does not age.

depicts.why: Wanting is pictured as the one thing in us that never tires

heals.why: Seeing that more years have not reduced the wanting loosens trust in it

commentary.reading: A verse found across the epic and in Bhartrihari's circle of ideas: the body decays, trishna stays young.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: One who lived off a tree in its good days should not abandon it when it has fallen on hard times.

depicts.why: The parrot speaks from loyalty to what once sheltered it

cultivates.why: Staying is the form gratitude takes
Holds to the bond through its hard season

commentary.reading: Indra praises the parrot's anrishamsya, non-cruelty and devotion, and revives the tree. The virtue is loyalty to a benefactor in decline, not staying with one who harms you.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Arrows can be drawn out of the body, but a harsh word lodges in the heart and cannot be removed.

depicts.why: The cruel word is pictured still lodged in the heart long after

cultivates.why: For the speaker, shows what a sentence does

commentary.reading: In context Bhishma is warning against harsh speech as part of good conduct; the same verse appears in Vidura Niti. It validates the hurt as real and lasting.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: A mother outweighs ten fathers and the whole earth in worth; there is no teacher equal to her.

cultivates.why: Places the mother above every other teacher

commentary.reading: A smriti-style ranking of gurus given by Bhishma: upadhyaya, acharya, father, mother.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Do not do to another what would be painful to yourself; this is dharma in brief.

heals.why: A single test to apply when the right course is unclear

cultivates.why: Uses one's own pain as the measure of another's
Dharma compressed to one question

commentary.reading: Brihaspati's samgrahika dharma, dharma in summary; conduct that departs from it springs from kama.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Destiny bears nothing without human effort, as seed bears nothing without a field.

heals.why: Removes fate as a reason not to act
Settles the fate versus effort doubt on the side of doing one's part

cultivates.why: Effort is the field in which anything can grow

commentary.reading: Brahma to Vasishtha on daiva and purushakara: both are needed, and effort is what a person holds.
commentary.source: Daiva-purushakara nirdesha, Anushasana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: The battle now before you needs no arrows or allies; it must be fought alone with your own mind.

heals.why: Names where the real struggle is
Tells a grieving king that the fight has moved inward

cultivates.why: Calls for taking up the inner fight
Addresses him as one able to fight it

commentary.reading: Krishna to Yudhishthira after the war: having beaten outer enemies he must now conquer the mind, or he will not be at peace.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: The two syllables 'mama', mine, are death; the three syllables 'na mama', not mine, are the eternal Brahman.

heals.why: Locates bondage in the single thought 'mine'
Possessiveness itself is called death

cultivates.why: Inner release of ownership while still acting
'Not mine' is identified with the eternal

needs: That one can hold duties and people without the claim of ownership

commentary.reading: Krishna tells Yudhishthira that giving up outer things does not free a person; giving up mamatva does. He is urging him to rule without possessiveness, not to leave for the forest.
commentary.source: Kama Gita context, Ashvamedhika Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

line_issue: 'Freedom' replaces 'the eternal Brahman'. Corrected: 'Mine: two syllables, and that is death. Not mine: three syllables, and that is the eternal.'

claim: Whoever gives according to his means, whether a hundred from a thousand or only water, earns equal merit.

heals.why: A small gift from small means is ranked equal to a large one
Removes size as the measure of worth

cultivates.why: What one has is enough to give from
Giving by capacity

commentary.reading: From the mongoose's tale: the gleaner's handful of barley flour outweighs Yudhishthira's Ashvamedha because it was given from true want with a pure heart.
commentary.source: Nakula (mongoose) upakhyana, Ashvamedhika Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Grey hair does not make an elder; the one who truly knows, even a child, is the elder.

depicts.why: Spoken by a boy turned away at the gate for his age

heals.why: Being dismissed for age or rank is answered with the true measure of worth

cultivates.why: Ashtavakra holds his ground without insult and asks to be judged on knowledge

commentary.reading: Ashtavakra at Janaka's gate; the same maxim is in Manu 2.156. He goes on to prove it by defeating Bandi in debate.
commentary.source: Ashtavakriya, Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Prosperity deludes even the wise and brave; one living in comfort does not notice it.

depicts.why: Said by a king who fell through this very blindness and now sees it

heals.why: Names the way success numbs self-awareness

cultivates.why: Watchfulness in good times

commentary.reading: Nahusha, fallen from Indra's seat into a python's body, speaks from experience of aishvarya-mada.
commentary.source: Ajagara parva, Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Never abandon dharma out of desire, rage or hatred; do not exult in the pleasant or burn at the unpleasant.

heals.why: Names rage as one of three forces that push a person off what is right

cultivates.why: Neither over-joy nor fever at events
Holding to dharma under pull

commentary.reading: The hunter's account of shishtachara, the conduct of the good.
commentary.source: Vyadha Gita (Dharmavyadha-Kaushika samvada), Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: Fix the mind on what is good and do not become wicked toward the wicked; remain good always.

heals.why: Refuses to let another's wrong decide one's own character

cultivates.why: Staying oneself under provocation
Goodness kept as one's own, not surrendered to the other's conduct

needs: The hurt has first been acknowledged; this does not ask for silence or for staying unprotected

commentary.reading: Shishtachara: the good do not answer papa with papa. It forbids becoming like the wrongdoer, not resisting him.
commentary.source: Vyadha Gita (Dharmavyadha-Kaushika samvada), Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: Remorse frees one from a wrong done, and resolving never to repeat it frees one from the next.

heals.why: Gives remorse a job and an end point

cultivates.why: The vow 'not again' is the second release

commentary.reading: The hunter on how wrongdoing is undone: anutapa, then the resolve of non-repetition. Parallel to Manu 11.230.
commentary.source: Vyadha Gita (Dharmavyadha-Kaushika samvada), Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: A person who turns to good after doing wrong is freed from it, like the moon from a cloud.

heals.why: The wrong is a cloud over the person, not the person
Worth is shown as recoverable

cultivates.why: Trust that turning to good actually clears the past

commentary.reading: Shishtachara teaching on release from papa by turning to kalyana.
commentary.source: Vyadha Gita (Dharmavyadha-Kaushika samvada), Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: Harm no being, live in friendliness, and having obtained this life make an enemy of no one.

heals.why: Enmity is weighed against the worth of a life

cultivates.why: Friendliness as the way of moving through life

commentary.reading: The hunter's closing counsel on ahimsa and maitri.
commentary.source: Vyadha Gita (Dharmavyadha-Kaushika samvada), Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

line_issue: 'This one life' adds 'one', which sits oddly with the text's worldview. Corrected: 'You have been given this life. Do not spend it in enmity with anyone.'

claim: A past benefactor who later offends, even gravely, should be forgiven on account of that earlier help.

heals.why: Sets remembered kindness on the scale beside the new hurt

cultivates.why: One of the named occasions where forgiveness is right
Old help is not erased by a later wrong

needs: The whole list: Prahlada also names when forgiveness must not be given

commentary.reading: Draupadi quotes Prahlada's list of times for kshama only to show its limits; she goes on to the times for tejas and says the Kauravas deserve none of this.
commentary.source: Draupadi-Yudhishthira samvada, Vana Parva (Prahlada-Bali itihasa quoted by Draupadi); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Neither force nor forgiveness is always the better course; each has its time.

heals.why: Releases the bind of feeling one must always forgive
Removes guilt for not being endlessly patient

cultivates.why: Asks which the time calls for
Firmness is given equal standing with forgiveness

commentary.reading: Draupadi, humiliated and exiled, cites Prahlada: one who always forgives is despised by servants and enemies alike, one who always uses force is feared and shunned. The teaching is fitness to time.
commentary.source: Draupadi-Yudhishthira samvada, Vana Parva (Prahlada-Bali itihasa quoted by Draupadi); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

line_issue: 'Wisdom is knowing which the moment needs' is a gloss, though true to the next verses. Closer: 'Force is not always right, and forgiveness is not always right. Know this for certain: both have their place.'

claim: One who does not return anger to the angry saves both himself and the other, and heals both.

heals.why: Shows the non-reply as protection for both sides

cultivates.why: Restraint pictured as medicine
The calm one is called the physician of both

commentary.reading: Yudhishthira's side of the forest debate. Draupadi and Bhima answer him, and the epic's whole arc is that peace was tried fully before the bow was taken up.
commentary.source: Yudhishthira's praise of kshama in the Draupadi-Yudhishthira samvada, Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Without people as forbearing as the earth there would be no reconciliation, because conflict is rooted in anger.

heals.why: Names anger as the root of quarrels

cultivates.why: Forbearance is what makes peace possible at all

commentary.reading: Yudhishthira's praise of kshama to Draupadi; one side of the debate, not its conclusion.
commentary.source: Yudhishthira's praise of kshama in the Draupadi-Yudhishthira samvada, Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: An angry person cannot tell what should or should not be said; nothing is beyond his doing or saying.

depicts.why: Pictures the angry mind for which nothing is off limits

heals.why: Shows what anger does to judgement before it acts

commentary.reading: Yudhishthira on the blindness of krodha. Said in reply to Draupadi's just indignation, so it must not be turned on someone who has been wronged.
commentary.source: Yudhishthira's praise of kshama in the Draupadi-Yudhishthira samvada, Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: A vow begun with resolve is carried through by that same resolve, so there is no cause for distress.

depicts.why: Savitri speaks from inside a decision already made

cultivates.why: Determination is named as the cause that carries the work
Calm under others' worry

commentary.reading: Savitri, knowing Satyavan is to die, undertakes the three-night vow and reassures her father-in-law. Vyavasaya, firm resolve, is the cause of success.
commentary.source: Savitri upakhyana (Pativrata-mahatmya), Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Even one meeting with the good is precious and never fruitless, so one should live in their company.

heals.why: Points toward good company as the remedy

cultivates.why: Friendship with the good is called the higher gain
Time with a good person always bears fruit

commentary.reading: Savitri to Yama as she follows him; her words on satsanga win his boons.
commentary.source: Savitri upakhyana (Pativrata-mahatmya), Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Ill will toward none in deed, thought or word, with kindness and giving, is the eternal dharma of the good.

heals.why: Adroha, no ill will, is set as the first mark of the good

cultivates.why: Goodwill in act, mind and speech
Anugraha, active kindness
Giving

commentary.reading: Savitri's definition of sanatana dharma to Yama.
commentary.source: Savitri upakhyana (Pativrata-mahatmya), Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: I do what is right because it ought to be done, not out of desire for its reward.

heals.why: Cuts right action loose from expected return
Answers 'why be good if it is not rewarded'

cultivates.why: Doing one's part as a householder to the best of one's ability
Dharma held for its own sake

needs: That the reader is asking why to keep doing right, not asking for their injury to be recognised

commentary.reading: Draupadi has asked why dharma has not protected them. Yudhishthira calls trading in dharma for reward the lowest attitude and says he acts because it is to be done.
commentary.source: Draupadi-Yudhishthira samvada, Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Kind speech makes one loved, considered action brings success, many friends bring happiness, devotion to dharma brings the goal.

cultivates.why: Kind speech and friendship are linked to being loved and at ease
Acting after thought

commentary.reading: One of the Yaksha's question sets; a generic niti answer.
commentary.source: Yaksha Prashna (Vana Parva); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Beings go to death every day, yet those remaining wish to stay forever; that is the greatest wonder.

heals.why: Exposes the daily assumption of unlimited time

cultivates.why: Seeing one's own denial clearly
Loosens the wish for permanence

commentary.reading: The famous 'kim ashcharyam' answer.
commentary.source: Yaksha Prashna (Vana Parva); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Reasoning is unsettled and authorities differ, so the path is the one the great have walked.

heals.why: Admits that argument and texts do not settle it, then gives a usable guide
When principles conflict, look to how the great have lived

cultivates.why: Trust in lived example over endless debate

commentary.reading: 'Mahajano yena gatah sa panthah': mahajana is traditionally taken as the great and good, not simply the crowd.
commentary.source: Yaksha Prashna (Vana Parva); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: The mind is faster than the wind and worries are more numerous than grass; mother and father outweigh earth and sky.

depicts.why: Worries counted as more than blades of grass
The mind outruns the wind

cultivates.why: Mother and father are ranked above earth and sky

commentary.reading: A Yaksha Prashna answer; the line uses its second half.
commentary.source: Yaksha Prashna (Vana Parva); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Competence is the best fortune, learning the best wealth, health the best gain, contentment the best happiness.

heals.why: Ranks contentment above every acquisition

cultivates.why: Tushti is named the highest happiness
Health counted as the best gain

commentary.reading: A Yaksha Prashna answer.
commentary.source: Yaksha Prashna (Vana Parva); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Giving up pride makes one loved, anger frees from grief, desire makes one rich, greed makes one happy.

heals.why: Pride is what stands between a person and being loved
Anger is tied to later sorrow
Greed is what blocks happiness

cultivates.why: Wealth is redefined as wanting less

commentary.reading: A Yaksha Prashna answer listing four renunciations and their fruits.
commentary.source: Yaksha Prashna (Vana Parva); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Anger is the hardest enemy to conquer and greed the endless disease; the good wish all beings well.

heals.why: Recasts anger as an opponent to be fought, not obeyed
Greed as an illness with no natural end

cultivates.why: The good are defined by goodwill to all beings

commentary.reading: A Yaksha Prashna answer.
commentary.source: Yaksha Prashna (Vana Parva); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: One who waits on fate without acting, sleeping at ease, sinks like an unbaked pot in water.

heals.why: Shows passivity dressed as trust in fate for what it is
Comfortable waiting ends in dissolving

cultivates.why: Draupadi insists that a person must act

commentary.reading: Draupadi, wronged and in exile, argues that neither fate nor chance replaces human effort; she calls the one who only waits a sudurbuddhi.
commentary.source: Draupadi's defence of purushakara (effort) to Yudhishthira, Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: A farmer who has done all that could be done is not at fault if rain fails, and should not blame himself.

depicts.why: Speaks to the one asking whether a failed result was their own doing

heals.why: Separates what was in one's hands from what was not
The rain was never the farmer's to command

cultivates.why: Having done one's part is the ground to stand on

commentary.reading: Draupadi's image for effort and what lies beyond it: the wise man reviews that he did what a person can do and does not reproach himself.
commentary.source: Draupadi's defence of purushakara (effort) to Yudhishthira, Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: Unrewarded effort is no reason for despair, since every action can end in either success or failure.

depicts.why: Quotes the thought itself: I keep working and nothing comes of it

heals.why: Weariness at unrewarded work is met by naming both possible ends
Failure is one of two normal outcomes, not a judgement

cultivates.why: Keeps the worker at the work

commentary.reading: Draupadi: nirveda should not be reached; action has two ends, and without action there is neither.
commentary.source: Draupadi's defence of purushakara (effort) to Yudhishthira, Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: A person should never despise himself, for one who holds himself in contempt does not reach real prosperity.

heals.why: Forbids self-contempt outright
Self-reproach is shown to block every good

cultivates.why: Self-respect is treated as the root of flourishing

commentary.reading: Draupadi, herself publicly humiliated, tells Yudhishthira that atma-avamana destroys bhuti. Spoken by the wronged, about not turning the wrong inward.
commentary.source: Draupadi's defence of purushakara (effort) to Yudhishthira, Vana Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: A parent who knows a child's wrongdoing and still follows the child's will is the one most to blame.

heals.why: Names fondness that has become blindness

cultivates.why: Love for a child does not excuse going along with wrong

commentary.reading: Gandhari, before the court, holds Dhritarashtra responsible for indulging Duryodhana.
commentary.source: Gandhari's counsel in the Kuru court, Udyoga Parva (Bhagavadyana); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: One must first conquer oneself as one would an enemy; then conquering advisers and rivals does not fail.

heals.why: Turns the contest inward, where it can be won

cultivates.why: Self-mastery first
Treats self-rule as a campaign

commentary.reading: Gandhari to Duryodhana on atma-jaya as the first victory of a ruler; recension readings of the second pada vary.
commentary.source: Gandhari's counsel in the Kuru court, Udyoga Parva (Bhagavadyana); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Greed never brings real wealth, so enough of greed; be at peace.

heals.why: A mother's plain word that greed does not deliver what it promises

cultivates.why: Be at peace is the instruction
Enough

commentary.reading: Gandhari's plea to Duryodhana to give the Pandavas their share.
commentary.source: Gandhari's counsel in the Kuru court, Udyoga Parva (Bhagavadyana); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: It is better to blaze briefly like a torch than to smoulder long without flame merely to stay alive.

heals.why: Half-living is pictured as smoke without flame
Sets wholehearted action above self-preservation

cultivates.why: Blaze
A life with flame in it

needs: The scene: a kshatriya mother rousing a defeated son to reclaim what was taken

commentary.reading: Vidula's most famous line: 'muhurtam jvalitam shreyo na tu dhumayitam chiram'. A call to a warrior's courage, told by Kunti to stir her sons. It makes light of clinging to life, so it must not reach someone in despair.
commentary.source: Vidula-putra-anushasana (the 'Jaya' itihasa told by Kunti), Udyoga Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: Whether he gains or fails, the wise person does not keep grieving but begins the next task at once.

heals.why: Loss is answered by the next beginning
Sorrow over an outcome is not allowed to become a dwelling

cultivates.why: Start what comes next immediately
Gain and failure get the same response

commentary.reading: Vidula: the pandita takes up the next thing without pause and does not treat his own life as wealth to be hoarded.
commentary.source: Vidula-putra-anushasana (the 'Jaya' itihasa told by Kunti), Udyoga Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: Do not despise yourself or settle for little; set your mind on the good and do not be afraid.

heals.why: Self-contempt after defeat is forbidden by a mother
Do not be afraid

cultivates.why: Refusing to shrink one's life to fit a defeat
Set the mind on what is truly good

commentary.reading: Vidula to her son, who lies down after being beaten by the Sindhu king. The wider speech shames him harshly; this verse is its constructive core.
commentary.source: Vidula-putra-anushasana (the 'Jaya' itihasa told by Kunti), Udyoga Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: Do not despise yourself for past failures, since fortunes arise and vanish; yet do not act from mere resentment.

heals.why: Past failure is not allowed to define the person
What was not can come to be

cultivates.why: Fortunes move, so the present low is not final
Warns against beginning from resentment alone

commentary.reading: Vidula softens after her son responds: wealth comes to those without it and leaves those with it; begin wisely, not out of amarsha.
commentary.source: Vidula-putra-anushasana (the 'Jaya' itihasa told by Kunti), Udyoga Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

line_issue: Line drops the closing caution. Fuller: 'Do not look down on yourself for past failures. Fortunes that never were arrive, and others are lost. Only do not begin out of resentment alone.'

claim: Every result is uncertain, yet those who act may succeed while those who never act never do.

heals.why: Fear of failing is weighed against the certainty of not trying
Uncertainty is admitted and made a reason to act

cultivates.why: Action is the only side with a chance
Decide to try

commentary.reading: Vidula: the fruit of action is always anitya; non-effort has one result only, absence.
commentary.source: Vidula-putra-anushasana (the 'Jaya' itihasa told by Kunti), Udyoga Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha not separately verified

claim: The drunk, heedless, exhausted, angry, hungry, hurried, greedy, frightened and lustful cannot see dharma, so avoid these states.

heals.why: Anger is listed as a state in which right and wrong cannot be seen
Fear likewise clouds judgement

cultivates.why: Check one's state before judging what is right

commentary.reading: Vidura's list of ten who do not know dharma. Some recensions and the Gita Press reading take the last line as 'do not keep company with such persons'; this edition reads 'these states'.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

line_issue: 'Don't decide' is an application, not the wording. Closer: 'Anger, exhaustion, hunger, hurry, greed and fear all hide what is right. Do not act from inside them.'

claim: Noble conduct does not rekindle a settled quarrel, mount on pride, or do wrong pleading hardship.

heals.why: Leave the quarrel that has gone quiet
Do not climb onto pride

cultivates.why: Hard times are not taken as licence
A calmed enmity is left calm

commentary.reading: Vidura's description of arya-shila.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: The wise grasp quickly, listen long, act from understanding and not desire, and do not intrude unasked.

cultivates.why: Listening long before acting
Staying out of what one was not asked into

commentary.reading: Vidura's first mark of the pandita.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: The wise do not long for the unattainable, grieve for what is lost, or lose clarity in calamity.

heals.why: Grieving the lost is named as something one can stop choosing
Longing for the unreachable
Clear head in calamity

cultivates.why: Composure under misfortune

commentary.reading: Vidura's description of pandita-buddhi; a generic maxim that describes more than it comforts.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: The wise person begins only after deciding, does not stop midway, wastes no time and stays self-controlled.

heals.why: Do not stall in the middle
Decide first, then move

cultivates.why: Nishchitya: begin from a settled decision
See the work through

commentary.reading: Vidura's mark of the pandita in action.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: The wise person is neither elated by honour nor pained by insult, and stays unshaken like a Ganga pool.

heals.why: Honour does not inflate
A slight is not allowed to set one's worth

cultivates.why: Same in honour and dishonour
The deep still pool

commentary.reading: Vidura's pandita, akshobhya like a deep pool of the Ganga.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: One who drags out tasks, doubts everything and is slow where speed is needed is a fool.

depicts.why: Doubting at every step
Stretching out what needs doing

commentary.reading: From Vidura's marks of the mudha; a verdict, safe only where the reader has asked to be pushed.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Blaming another for one's own fault, and raging when powerless, mark the greatest fool.

heals.why: Anger without power to act is shown as self-harm

commentary.reading: Vidura's mudhatama. The second half would wound someone who is powerless against a real wrong.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: The forgiving have one fault, being thought weak, but forgiveness is the supreme strength and an ornament of the strong.

heals.why: Answers the fear that forgiving makes one look weak

cultivates.why: Forgiveness is called param balam
In the strong it is an ornament, chosen from strength

needs: A reader who has already chosen to forgive and doubts it; never as an instruction to someone wronged

commentary.reading: Vidura's praise of kshama. The Mahabharata sets this beside Prahlada's teaching that forgiveness is not always right.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: One who seeks prosperity must give up sleep, drowsiness, fear, anger, laziness and procrastination.

heals.why: Laziness and dirgha-sutrata, putting off, are named faults
Drowsiness as a habit

cultivates.why: Clears what stands in the way of rising

commentary.reading: Vidura's six doshas. Sleep here means excess sleep.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Health, freedom from debt, living at home, good company, one's own livelihood and fearless living are the six joys.

heals.why: The list has no luxury in it

cultivates.why: Happiness counted in six plain things
Lets a reader notice which of the six they already have

commentary.reading: Vidura's six sukhas of the living world. Avipravasa is not having to live away from home, which may sting readers abroad.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: The envious, the scornful, the discontented, the irritable, the ever suspicious and the dependent are always unhappy.

heals.why: Envy is first on the list of standing causes of unhappiness
Short temper listed as a constant sorrow

cultivates.why: By contrast, contentment is the way out

commentary.reading: Vidura's six nitya-duhkhitas. 'Ghrini' is read here as one given to aversion.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: When a task done by right method and means still fails, the wise person should not let his mind sink.

heals.why: Right effort that failed is not a fault
The mind is told not to droop

cultivates.why: Steadiness after a clean failure

commentary.reading: Vidura on action: when upaya and yoga were sound and the work still did not succeed, the medhavi does not let the mind wilt.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: When the foolish abuse the wise, the abuser takes on the wrong and the one who bears it is freed.

heals.why: The insult is shown to stain the speaker, not the target
Removes the need to hit back in order to be clean

cultivates.why: Bearing is pictured as release
Abuse does not transfer to the one abused

commentary.reading: Vidura on akrosha and parivada: the speaker takes up the papa and the forbearing one is released from his own.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: A forest cut by arrows or axe grows back, but a wound made by harsh words does not heal.

depicts.why: The word-wound is pictured as the one injury that does not close

cultivates.why: For the speaker, the permanence of what a sentence does

commentary.reading: Vidura's warning against harsh speech; it also tells the wounded that the wound is real.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: The gods do not guard with a staff like herdsmen; they give sound judgement to those they wish to protect.

heals.why: Answers 'why does no one protect me' by pointing to the judgement one has been given
Protection is located in clear thinking

cultivates.why: Good judgement is treated as divine protection itself
Help arrives as clarity

commentary.reading: Vidura: daiva protects through buddhi; the paired verse says those the gods would ruin lose their judgement.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Gold is tested by fire, character by conduct, courage by danger, and friends and enemies by hard times.

heals.why: Explains why hard times thin out one's circle
Hardship is recast as the test that shows what is real

cultivates.why: Read people by what they do in difficulty
The steady one is known in want

commentary.reading: Vidura's tests of character.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Do by day what lets you sleep at night, and in youth what lets you live at ease in age.

heals.why: Ties tonight's rest to today's conduct
A simple daily test for a clear conscience

cultivates.why: Choose today's act by how it will sit at night
Each stretch of time prepares the next

commentary.reading: Said to a king who cannot sleep because of what he has allowed; the full verse extends to doing lifelong what gives peace after death.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: One whose anger you fear or whom you must approach warily is no friend; a friend is trusted like a father.

depicts.why: Describes the relationship in which one is always watching the other's temper

heals.why: Names that fear as a sign about the bond, not a flaw in oneself
Walking on eggshells is not what friendship asks

cultivates.why: A test for which bonds are real
Permission to stop appeasing

commentary.reading: Vidura's definition of mitra: one in whom you rest as in a father; the others are sangatani, mere associations.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Brooding destroys beauty, strength and understanding and brings illness, and grief gains nothing, so do not dwell in it.

heals.why: Counts what brooding takes: strength, judgement, health
Grief is shown as costly and without yield

commentary.reading: Vidura on santapa and shoka to the anxious king.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: There is no peace apart from learning, austerity, restraint of the senses and giving up greed.

depicts.why: The king says it himself: everything is always unsettled and this mind is always unsettled
He asks for the state that is free of agitation

heals.why: Vidura answers the restless mind with four concrete supports

cultivates.why: Peace is said to come only by these means

commentary.reading: Dhritarashtra's question is one of the plainest statements of anxiety in the epic; Vidura's reply names vidya, tapas, indriya-nigraha and lobha-tyaga.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

line_issue: Line keeps only the answer and drops the king's question, which is the Day 1 hook. Add: 'Everything feels unsettled, and my mind is never at rest. Tell me, wise one, where is the place free of this unrest?'

claim: Anger is a bitter, burning drink that the good swallow and the bad cannot; drink it and be calm.

heals.why: Anger is pictured as something one can swallow instead of spill

cultivates.why: Swallowing it is the mark of the good

commentary.reading: The Sanskrit word is manyu. Vidura asks the king, who holds the power, to swallow his own resentment; it is not counsel to the injured party.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Whatever one constantly practises in deed, thought and word carries one along, so practise the good.

heals.why: Shows that repetition is quietly steering the person
Habit, not fate, is what pulls

cultivates.why: Choose what to repeat

commentary.reading: Vidura on abhyasa: what is frequented takes the person over.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: A gain that leads to loss is not to be prized, and a loss that leads to gain is.

heals.why: Gives a longer measure for weighing a choice
Not every gain is worth having

cultivates.why: Judge by where a thing leads

commentary.reading: Vidura on vriddhi and kshaya.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: The crooked-minded take a straightforward, modest person for weak and so mistreat him.

depicts.why: Describes being pushed around precisely because one is decent
Being taken for weak

heals.why: The fault is placed with the small-minded, not with one's honesty

commentary.reading: Vidura: arjava and modesty are misread as incapacity by the kubuddhi, who then insult the person.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Dharma must never be abandoned out of desire, fear or greed, not even to save one's life.

heals.why: One fixed point when pressure comes from desire, fear or gain
Fear is named and refused as a reason

cultivates.why: Holding to what is right at cost
Integrity that cannot be bought or frightened

commentary.reading: Vidura calls this his highest word, the punya pada; the verse is the heart of the 'Bharata Savitri'.
commentary.source: Vidura Niti (Udyoga Parva, Prajagara); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: One who takes the self to be other than what it is has robbed himself and committed every wrong.

heals.why: Mistaking what one is is named as the root error

cultivates.why: Points to knowing the self as it is

commentary.reading: In the Sanatsujatiya the verse is read of self-ignorance: holding the self, which is one way, to be another. The same verse in Adi Parva is used by Shakuntala of a man who denies what he knows. The line follows the second, social sense.
commentary.source: Shankara's Sanatsujatiya-bhashya and Nilakantha, recalled and not checked against the text

line_issue: Line reads it as social pretence; in this setting it is about mistaking one's own nature. Alternative: 'To take yourself for something other than what you truly are is a theft, and what is stolen is your own self.'

claim: Victory breeds enmity and the defeated lie in pain; one who has set aside victory and defeat sleeps in peace.

heals.why: Shows that winning the quarrel does not end it
The one carrying enmity sleeps badly

cultivates.why: Peace is placed beyond winning and losing
Setting down both outcomes

commentary.reading: Yudhishthira, the wronged party, makes the fullest case for peace before Krishna's embassy. The arc must stay whole: peace is offered to the last, refused, and then the war is fought.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Enmity is never ended by enmity; it only grows, like fire fed with ghee.

heals.why: Retaliation is shown to feed what it means to end

cultivates.why: Only a non-hostile response can close it

commentary.reading: Yudhishthira to Krishna before the embassy; one side of a deliberation that ends in a just war after peace fails.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: People despise the soft and recoil from the harsh, so be neither only harsh nor only mild but both in season.

depicts.why: Names the experience of being walked over for being gentle

heals.why: Gentleness alone is said to invite contempt, which lifts the blame from the gentle

cultivates.why: Firmness is given a rightful place
Knowing which the moment needs

commentary.reading: Brihaspati to Indra on holding authority: tikshna when needed, mridu when needed. The speaker attribution follows the library.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Bear the prosperity of others even when you lack it, for fortune drains away from one who resents.

heals.why: Resentment of others' fortune is shown to drive one's own away

cultivates.why: The skilled can take joy in good fortune that sits elsewhere
Ease with what others have

commentary.reading: The sage to the deposed prince: tolerate the shri of others.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Honouring mother, father and teachers is the most esteemed duty and brings great renown.

cultivates.why: Reverence toward those who raised and taught one
Honour shown in conduct

commentary.reading: Bhishma's answer on the highest duty. The library deliberately omits the next verses on obeying them in everything.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: One who slanders others before a crowd only displays his own faults, like a snake raising its hood.

heals.why: The public insult is turned back on the one who made it
The slandered person is not the one exposed

cultivates.why: No need to answer in kind to keep one's standing
The crowd sees the slanderer

commentary.reading: Bhishma answers how a learned, mild man should take a fool's abuse in the assembly. The surrounding advice is to stay silent and unshaken; this verse supplies the reason.
commentary.source: Bhishma on bearing a fool's abuse in the assembly (Shanti Parva, Rajadharma); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: The praise or blame of a senseless person achieves nothing, like a crow cawing in the forest.

heals.why: Mindless blame is given no weight
The abuse is reduced to noise

cultivates.why: Praise and blame from the careless are equally empty

commentary.reading: Bhishma on the abuser in the assembly: his words are without sense or effect. Fair criticism is a different matter.
commentary.source: Bhishma on bearing a fool's abuse in the assembly (Shanti Parva, Rajadharma); plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: A wise enemy is better than a foolish friend.

cultivates.why: Judge allies by sense, not by label

commentary.reading: The mouse Palita reasons that his life now depends on the cat, his natural enemy. Apaddharma: alliances in an emergency. A generic maxim outside the story.
commentary.source: Marjara-mushika samvada, Shanti Parva Apaddharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Gentleness overcomes both the gentle and the harsh, so nothing is beyond it and it is the sharper weapon.

heals.why: Offers gentleness as the more effective tool

cultivates.why: Softness used deliberately

commentary.reading: From the hard-headed statecraft Bharadvaja teaches King Shatrunjaya, where gentleness is a means of prevailing. Not a teaching on meekness.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: A wife is her husband's companion in dharma, livelihood and love, and the one he trusts when far from home.

cultivates.why: Names all a life partner is
Marriage as companionship in every pursuit

commentary.reading: The pigeon's praise of his wife as sahayini in dharma, artha and kama.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

line_issue: Sanskrit speaks of the wife as the man's helper; the line's neutral 'partner' is the right handling and should be kept.

claim: Desire cannot be filled in a day, in months, or even in a lifetime of trying.

depicts.why: The unfillable want, pictured as a vessel no lifetime can fill

heals.why: Seeing it cannot be filled ends the project of filling it
More will not be enough

cultivates.why: Rest is not on the far side of getting

commentary.reading: Yudhishthira to Bhima while arguing for renunciation; his family answers him and he rules. The observation about iccha stands on its own.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

line_issue: 'Stop trying to fill it' is added. Corrected: 'Wanting cannot be filled in a day, or in months. Even a whole lifetime of filling it would not be enough.'

claim: The ungrateful have no good name, standing or happiness, cannot be trusted, and have no expiation.

heals.why: For one betrayed by someone they helped, the text sides with them plainly

cultivates.why: Shows what is lost when gratitude is lost

commentary.reading: Bhishma's verdict on Gautama the kritaghna: for ingratitude there is no nishkriti.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Gaining a friend is better than gaining wealth, since wealth comes through friends and with a friend one can strive.

heals.why: Wealth is placed second

cultivates.why: Friendship ranked above money

commentary.reading: Bhishma closing the Gautama story.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

line_issue: 'Money comes and goes' is not in the verse. Corrected: 'A friend is a greater gain than money. Money comes easily through friends, and with a friend you can attempt anything.'

claim: Whatever is taken as 'mine' becomes a cause of anguish when it is lost.

heals.why: Shows the sense of 'mine' as the handle by which loss hurts
Explains the size of the pain without denying it

cultivates.why: Seeing the mechanism of mamatva

commentary.reading: The brahmin to Senajit: mamatva is the seed of paritapa.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: No one knows whose death comes today, so one should live by dharma while still young.

heals.why: Removes the assumption of later

cultivates.why: Begin right living now

commentary.reading: Medhavin to his father: life is anitya, so dharma is not for old age.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: The world is struck by death and ringed by old age while days and nights fall away; why do you not wake?

heals.why: A direct call out of drift

cultivates.why: Seeing time as it passes

commentary.reading: Medhavin's opening challenge to his father; the dialogue presses toward moksha over household stages.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: The wealthy are always anxious, as if in the jaws of death, which is the great difference from having nothing.

heals.why: Wealth is shown to bring fear with it
Money anxiety is traced to holding, not lacking

cultivates.why: Having little is recast as freedom

commentary.reading: Shampaka, a destitute brahmin, praises akinchanya over kingship. A renunciate's voice.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

line_issue: Line softens to 'can come with'. Closer: 'Between having nothing and having a kingdom there is one great difference: the wealthy are always anxious.'

claim: Without giving up there is no happiness, no highest goal and no fearless sleep; give up everything and be happy.

heals.why: Clinging is named as what stands between a person and rest
Fearless sleep is tied to letting go

cultivates.why: Tyaga as the single condition

commentary.reading: Shampaka: 'tyaktva sarvam sukhi bhavet'. Literal total renunciation; the line wisely keeps only the first half.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: Because nothing is mine my wealth is endless, and if Mithila burns nothing of mine burns.

heals.why: Ownership dropped while the kingdom is still ruled
Nothing to lose because nothing is claimed

cultivates.why: Inner non-possession in the midst of responsibility
Fearlessness before loss

needs: Janaka is a ruling king; this is non-possessiveness, not indifference

commentary.reading: Janaka's famous utterance, quoted as the model of one free while acting in the world.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: An osprey carrying meat is attacked by others and finds peace by dropping it.

heals.why: The prize is shown as the reason for the attack
What everyone fights over may not be worth carrying

cultivates.why: Peace comes with the dropping

commentary.reading: One of Bodhya's teachers; the same image is in the Bhagavata's Avadhuta Gita.
commentary.source: Bodhya Gita, Shanti Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: I neither refuse a rightful enjoyment that comes unsought nor pursue one that is hard to obtain.

heals.why: No chasing
Nothing depends on getting the rare thing

cultivates.why: Receives what arrives, in keeping with dharma

commentary.reading: The sage of the ajagara vow to Prahlada. An ascetic's rule, but this verse states a contentment a householder can keep.
commentary.source: Ajagara-Prahlada samvada, Shanti Parva; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: Gaining what one wants gives no satisfaction; craving blazes higher, like fire fed with fuel.

depicts.why: The want that grows each time it is fed

heals.why: Getting is shown as fuel, not cure
Removes the hope that one more will settle it

commentary.reading: The jackal to Kashyapa; a stock verse on trishna.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: It does not befit one who has everything to boast over one who has lost everything.

depicts.why: Bali, fallen, is being gloated over to his face

heals.why: Being low is not being lesser

cultivates.why: He names the gloating as unworthy without begging or raging

commentary.reading: Bali's first reply to Indra's mockery.
commentary.source: Bali-Vasava-samvada, Shanti Parva Mokshadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

line_issue: Line turns Bali's reply into a general maxim. Keep his voice: 'It does not suit your name or your family to boast over me, when you have everything and I have lost it.'

claim: This is a time for calm, not for valour; Time establishes and ripens everything.

heals.why: A low season is read as a season

cultivates.why: Waiting without bitterness
Calm fitted to the time

commentary.reading: Bali's doctrine of Kala: he does not fight now because the time is against him, and tells Indra his turn will also pass.
commentary.source: Bali-Vasava-samvada, Shanti Parva Mokshadharma; plain sense as in the Gita Press Hindi rendering

claim: For all born beings meeting and parting are certain, arising and vanishing like bubbles on water.

heals.why: Parting is placed inside the nature of meeting
Bonds seen as bubbles

cultivates.why: What comes together separates

commentary.reading: Vyasa to Yudhishthira, who wishes to fast to death in grief.
commentary.source: Plain sense of the verse as in the Gita Press Hindi Mahabharata; Nilakantha's gloss not separately verified

claim: One who is always a friend to all and devoted to their good in deed, mind and speech knows dharma.
